subject: health
title: Guided practice: confidentiality and consent concepts
essentialQuestion: How can understanding health systems, information, and self-advocacy help us explain, decide, create, or solve something that matters?
materials: unit-specific source, model, manipulatives, safe materials, or approved digital tool
keyPoints: Consent and confidentiality are related but different: consent concerns permission for care, while confidentiality concerns who may receive information; both have legal and safety limits.
Match the need to the appropriate service, ask how consent and confidentiality work in that setting, identify access constraints, and confirm the next step before sharing details.
For confidentiality and consent concepts, a strong response distinguishes fact from assumption, uses a fictional or public case, and includes a safe next step or appropriate source of support.
privacySafeScenario: Create a reliable-information and self-advocacy toolkit using fictional scenarios.
studentTask: Route two supplied fictional needs involving confidentiality and consent concepts. For each, choose the appropriate service, list two consent, confidentiality, cost, or access questions, and write the next action the fictional person can take without revealing unrelated details.
knowledgeCheck: In two or three sentences, explain the most important distinction in confidentiality and consent concepts; use one lesson fact and name the evidence, safety check, or support route that makes the explanation dependable.
completionCriteria: The response completes every named part of the confidentiality and consent concepts task using the supplied fictional or public case.
The response uses at least two accurate details from the lesson instruction and distinguishes evidence from assumption.
The response gives a safe, feasible next step or support route and does not depend on private disclosure, body comparison, or recorded media proof.
